summary: Clarifies the standards status of the documents that define forward and reverse mapping of IPv6 addresses in the DNS. It moves the A6 record and bit-string label specifications to experimental status. It updates RFCs 2673 and 2874 and was later updated by RFC 6672.

eli5.summary: There were two competing ways to store the new longer addresses in the internet's phone book. This document says one way is now just an experiment.

questions: what happened to the a6 record
how are ipv6 addresses stored in dns
subtitle: The IETF settles the AAAA versus A6 argument: AAAA for production, A6 and bit labels demoted to experiments.

tldr.problem: Two competing ways of storing IPv6 addresses in the DNS (AAAA and A6) were both Proposed Standards, and the confusion was seen as a threat to IPv6 deployment.
tldr.mechanism: Based on working group discussion, the memo recommends that AAAA stay on the standards track while A6 (RFC 2874) and binary bit labels (RFC 2673) move to Experimental status, and that DNAME in the reverse tree be deprecated.
tldr.outcome: AAAA became the recommended choice for production IPv6 deployment, while A6 and bit labels were left as experiments. The memo was later updated by RFC 6672.

facts.label: Meeting behind the consensus
facts.value: Joint DNSEXT and NGTRANS, 51st IETF, August 2001

today: RFC 3363 is an Informational memo that updates RFC 2673 and RFC 2874, and it was later updated by RFC 6672. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Decision Was Needed
sections.content:
By 2002 the IETF had begun standardizing two different ways to put an IPv6 address in the DNS: the AAAA record (RFC 1886) and the A6 record (RFC 2874). Both were Proposed Standards. The memo says this led to confusion and conflicts over which one to deploy, and that having more than one choice could delay the deployment of IPv6.

The goal is simply to clarify the situation. The memo is based on discussion on several working group mailing lists and on a joint DNSEXT and NGTRANS meeting at the 51st IETF in August 2001. The detailed arguments are in a separate document, RFC 3364; this memo summarizes the outcome. Who runs the root of the reverse IPv6 map is out of scope and is covered by RFC 3152.

In the standards action section, the memo states that it changes the status of RFCs 2673 and 2874 from Proposed Standard to Experimental.
sections.eli5: Two groups invented two different ways to write long internet addresses in the internet's phone book. People got confused about which to use, so this memo steps in to sort it out.

sections.title: AAAA Versus A6
sections.content:
The perceived consensus of the DNSEXT and NGTRANS chairs was that AAAA records are preferable for production deployment of IPv6 at the moment, that A6 records have interesting properties that need to be better understood before deployment, and that it is not known whether the benefits of A6 outweigh the costs and risks.

The rationale centers on the feature that makes A6 different: chaining, where an address is built up from several records. Resolving an N-link chain means resolving a series of nearly independent queries, so the time is expected to be roughly proportional to N, and the chance of failure also appears to be roughly proportional to N. The memo worries that users, already impatient with DNS lookups for IPv4, would not tolerate much longer delays.

A further concern is that the most interesting uses of A6 point at targets in other zones run by other organizations. The memo notes that experience with glue records and with PTR records in the IN-ADDR.ARPA tree suggests that pointers to other organizations are often not maintained properly.

The recommendation: RFC 1886 stays on the standards track and is advanced, while RFC 2874 moves to Experimental.
sections.eli5: The fancy way builds an address by asking many other places for pieces, like a scavenger hunt. Every extra stop takes time and can go wrong, so the simple way, where the whole address sits in one place, wins for now.

sections.title: Bit Labels in the Reverse Tree
sections.content:
RFC 2673 defined a new kind of DNS label, the binary (bit) label, the first new label type since RFC 1035. The memo reports that deploying a new label type turned out to be difficult, because DNS servers that do not support bit labels reject queries containing them as malformed. The community also indicated that this label type is not needed for mapping reverse addresses.

The reasoning is that the hexadecimal text representation of IPv6 addresses appears able to express all of the delegation schemes expected to be used in the reverse DNS tree.

The recommended action is to change the status of RFC 2673 from Proposed to Experimental. Any future standardization is left to the DNSEXT working group or its successor.
sections.eli5: Someone invented a brand new kind of label for the phone book, but older phone book machines choked on it. Since the normal way of writing the numbers already works, the new label is put on the shelf as an experiment.

sections.title: DNAME in the IPv6 Reverse Tree
sections.content:
The memo says the question of DNAME records in the reverse mapping tree is closely tied to the need for fragmented A6 in the main tree: if one is necessary, so is the other, and if one is not, the other is not either.

Therefore, in moving RFC 2874 to Experimental, the intent of the memo is that the use of DNAME RRs in the reverse tree be deprecated.
sections.eli5: A DNAME is a shortcut sign in the phone book. Because the shortcut only mattered for the fancy address method, it goes away from the reverse phone book too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Because the document specifies a course of action, it says there are no direct security considerations. It does note an indirect impact of the choice: the relationship between A6 and DNSSEC is not well understood throughout the community, while choosing AAAA leads to a model for using DNSSEC in IPv6 networks that parallels current IPv4 practice. The memo has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is being built here, so there is nothing new to break into. Sticking with the simpler method just keeps the lock-and-key rules the same as before.
